prize_parts.citation: For a visionary, densely patterned body of prose and poetry that turns memory, the body and dream into an inner cosmos of rare formal ambition.

statement.case_for: My opening ranking stands after rereading the colleagues' arguments. Cărtărescu offers the strongest combination under the common criteria. The voice is distinctive and recognisable. The prose is dense and patterned, and it treats memory, the body and dream as a single imaginative system. Blinding (the first volume of the Orbitor trilogy) and Solenoid show formal ambition and intellectual depth at large scale, and the poetry and essays suggest range beyond the major novels. The architecture of the project appears to be coherent rather than merely accumulated, and the work extends a European line of encyclopedic and oneiric fiction while remaining his own. The attribution is clean: one writer, one language, and a citation that can cover the whole oeuvre without separating strands. I weigh these as literary reasons. The fact that colleagues' openings point the same way is not a merit argument, and I do not use it as one.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that the achievement is tied closely to the rhythm and syntax of Romanian prose. I cannot judge how much survives in translation. My knowledge of the poetry, the essays and the early work is also thinner than my knowledge of the major novels. The maximalism may conceal unevenness across volumes, and that would count against sustained quality if it proved true on closer reading. I have not read the corpus independently or verified sources, so these are open questions rather than settled judgments.

responses.point: Carlberg ranks Adonis second. She sees a major modernizer of Arabic poetic language who worked through myth, fragmentation and dialogue with the classical tradition, and she notes that his criticism reinforces his influence.
responses.response: I take the case seriously, and I ranked him seventh with real uncertainty. The renewal of a whole poetic language is a significant achievement under the formal and linguistic criterion. My hesitation is that Arabic prosody and the relation to classical forms are very hard to judge in translation, and that his influence as a critic and anthologist can be mistaken for the intrinsic achievement of the poems. Carlberg's own caveat that the essays should support the poetry and not carry the case is the point I would press. If she or others can show from the poems themselves, beyond their influence, that the late work keeps its force, I would revise my ranking upward. I have not yet seen that argument made.

responses.point: Olsson ranks Anne Carson second and describes rare formal inventiveness joining scholarship, lyric, verse novel and visual form. He also flags that her translations and performance pieces sit awkwardly with an oeuvre-based assessment.
responses.response: I agree with the formal case. Autobiography of Red and Nox are original reinventions of genre, and I ranked her third. I also share his reservation about scope. A citation would have to say clearly what counts as the oeuvre, and the hybrid works make classification contestable. Where I differ is on the weight of that problem. I think it is a drafting difficulty more than a literary weakness. It does make her a less secure single-writer citation than Cărtărescu, whose scope is unambiguous. I keep her as an alternative for that reason and not as my first choice.

responses.point: Sem-Sandberg ranks Yoko Tawada third. He argues that her bilingual practice is central to the writing, not a biographical detail, and that it turns linguistic estrangement into form across several genres.
responses.response: This is the argument that most affects my view of Tawada. I ranked her sixth, and the formal and linguistic case is strong in principle. My difficulty is practical. The wordplay at the centre of her method has to be judged in Japanese and German, and neither of us can claim direct access to both. His own caveat that coverage of the shorter and poetic work is thin applies to me as well. I also read some of the work as lighter in scale than the largest candidates, though I could be wrong about that. I do not want to prefer her over Cărtărescu on evidence I cannot weigh, but I would want the committee to test whether the bilingual project deepens over time.

responses.point: Mattson ranks Cărtărescu first as a sustained architect of inner worlds. She warns that his work may seem over-extended in places and that the quality of the dense Romanian prose in translation may differ from the original.
responses.response: I share both reservations and have included them in my own case against. I read the risk of over-extension as a question about specific volumes and not about the project as a whole, and the committee can examine it directly. Her point that the major structures are complete enough to judge supports the claim that the oeuvre is mature. I would add that the translation uncertainty cannot be resolved by discussion alone. It remains a limit on how confident any of us can be about the sentence-level achievement.

responses.point: Sward ranks Can Xue second and Carson third. She argues that Can Xue's formal radicalism is part of the imaginative vision, not a surface device, but that it is hard to judge whether the later work deepens the mode or repeats it.
responses.response: I agree, and this is the same question I raised about sameness of method. It is why I place Can Xue second and not first. The originality is real, and I regard it as one of the most uncompromising projects on the list. The open issue is whether decades of work in a single dream-logic mode yield enough development and variety, and the partial translated corpus prevents any of us from answering confidently. I hold her as my first alternative on the strength of that originality. I accept her point that the question remains unresolved.

uncertainties: How much of the effect of Cărtărescu's dense Romanian prose survives in translation, and whether translated coverage of the poetry, essays and early work is adequate.
Whether quality is consistent across the long volumes of the late novels or uneven in places.
Whether Can Xue's sustained single mode develops or repeats over the whole corpus, given partial translation.
How the committee should treat Carson's hybrid works, translations and performance pieces in an oeuvre-based citation.
Whether the late work of Adonis keeps its force independently of his influence as a critic, given the limits of translating Arabic prosody.
I have not read the corpora independently or verified sources, and my judgments rest on public knowledge of representative works.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile. My documented connections (election alongside David Håkansson, work with Kate Larson, my biography of Selma Lagerlöf) do not relate to any shortlisted writer. My own literary practice is context only and is not treated as evidence for any preference.
